metadata.title: Blow up and Blur constructions in algebraic logic

nodes.name: Closure of subneat reduct classes under completions
nodes.statement: We discuss the possibility of obtaining stronger results concerning completions, for example we approach the problem as to whether classes of subneat reducts are closed under completions, and analogous results for infinite dimensions.
nodes.statement_short: Are classes of subneat reducts closed under completions (and what about infinite dimensions)?

nodes.name: Split and blur method
nodes.statement: The main idea is to {\it split and blur}. Split what? You can split a clique by taking $\omega$ many disjoint copies of it, you can split a finite relation algebra, by splitting each atom into $\omega$ many, you can split a finite cylindric algebra. Generally, the splitting has to do with blowing up a finite structure into infinitely many. Then blur what? On this split one adds a subset of a set of fixed in advance blurs, usually finite, and then define an infinite atom structure, induced by the properties of the finite structure he originally started with. It is not this atom structure that is blurred but rather the original finite structure. This means that the term algebra built on this new atom structure, that is the algebra generated by the atoms, coincides with a carefully chosen partition of the set of atoms obtained after splittig and bluring up to minimal deviations, so the original finite relation algebra is blurred to the extent that is invisible on this level.
nodes.statement_short: Split a finite structure into infinitely many atoms, then add blurs so the term algebra no longer sees the finite structure.

nodes.name: Term algebra representable, complex algebra not
nodes.statement: The term algebra will be representable, using all such blurs as colours, But the original algebra structure re-appears in the completion of this term algebra, that is the complex algebra of the atom structure, forcing it to be non representable, due to a finite-infinite discrepancy. However, if the blurs are infinite, then, they will blur also the structure of the small algebra in the complex algebra, and the latter will be representable, inducing a complete representation of the term algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Finitely many blurs: term algebra representable but its completion is not; infinitely many blurs: completion representable too.

nodes.name: Atom structure (convention)
nodes.statement: In what follows, by an atom structure, we mean an atom structure of any class of completely additive Boolean algebras.

nodes.name: Splitting, blur, and blown up and blurred atom structure
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item A splitting of $N$ is a disjoint union $N\times I$, where $I$ is an infinite set. \item A blur for $N$ is any set $J$. \item An atom structure $\alpha$ is blown up and blurred if, there exists a subset $J'$ of a set $J$ of blurs, possibly empty, such that $\alpha$ has underlying set $X=N\times I \times J'$; the latter atom structure is called a blur of $N$ via $J$, and is denoted by $\alpha(N,J).$ Furthermore, every $j\in J$, induces a non-principal ultrafilter in $\wp(X)$. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ reflects $N$, if $N$ is faithfully represented in $\Cm\alpha(N,J)$ \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is weak if $\Tm\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ is very weak $\Tm\alpha(N,J)$ is not representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is strong if $\Cm\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: Defines splittings $N\times I$, blurs $J$, the blown up and blurred atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$, and when it reflects $N$ or is weak, very weak or strong.
nodes.definiendum: blown up and blurred atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$

nodes.name: Two examples of weak atom structures
nodes.statement: We give two examples of weak atom structures. The first construction builds two relativized set algebras based on a certain model that is in turn a Fraisse limit of a class of certain labelled graphs, with the labels coming from $\G\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, where $\G$ is an arbitrary graph and $\rho$ is a new colour. Under certain conditions on $\G$, the first set algebra can be represented on square units, the second, its completion, cannot.

nodes.name: Family $\cal F$ of labelled graphs
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be a graph. One can define a family of labelled graphs $\cal F$ such that every edge of each graph $\Gamma\in {\cal F}$, is labelled by a unique label from $\G\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $\rho\notin \G$, in a carefully chosen way. The colour of $(\rho, i)$ is defined to be $i$. The \textit{colour} of $(a, i)$ for $a \in \G$ is $i$. $\cal F$ consists of all complete labelled graphs $\Gamma$ (possibly the empty graph) such that for all distinct $ x, y, z \in \Gamma$, writing $ (a, i) = \Gamma (y, x)$, $ (b, j) = \Gamma (y, z)$, $ (c,l) = \Gamma (x, z)$, we have:\\ \begin{enumarab} \item $| \{ i, j, l \} > 1 $, or \item $ a, b, c \in \G$ and $ \{ a, b, c \} $ has at least one edge of $\G$, or \item exactly one of $a, b, c$ -- say, $a$ -- is $\rho$, and $bc$ is an edge of $\G$, or \item two or more of $a, b, c$ are $\rho$. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: Complete graphs labelled by $\G\cup\{\rho\}\times n$ whose triangles satisfy one of four colour/edge conditions.
differentia: $ a, b, c \in \G$ and $ \{ a, b, c \} $ has at least one edge of $\G$, or
exactly one of $a, b, c$ -- say, $a$ -- is $\rho$, and $bc$ is an edge of $\G$, or
two or more of $a, b, c$ are $\rho$.

nodes.name: Labelled graph $M$ as a model
nodes.statement: One forms a labelled graph $M$ which can be viewed as model of a natural signature, namely, the one with relation symbols $R_{(a, i)}$, for each $a \in \G \cup \{\rho\}$, $i<n$ and

nodes.name: Set $W$ of permitted assignments
nodes.statement: Then one takes a subset $W\subseteq {}^nM$, by roughly dropping assignments that do not satify $(\rho, l)$ for every $l<n$. Formally, $W = \{ \bar{a} \in {}^n M : M \models ( \bigwedge_{i < j < n, l < n} \neg (\rho, l)(x_i, x_j))(\bar{a}) \}.$ Basically, we are throwing away assignments $\bar{a}$ whose edges betwen two of its elements are labelled by $\rho$, and keeping those whose edges of its elements are not.
nodes.statement_short: $W$ = the $n$-tuples of $M$ no two of whose elements are joined by a $\rho$-labelled edge.

nodes.name: Choices of the graph $\G$
nodes.statement: Now for particular choices of $\G$; for example if $\G$ is a certain rainbow graph, or more simply a countable infinite collection of pairwise union of disjoint $N$ cliques with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$, or is the graph whose nodes are the natural numbers, and the edge relation is defined by $iEj$ iff $0<|i-j|<N$, for same $N.$ Here, the choice of $N$ is not haphazard, but it a bound of edges of complete graphs having $n$ nodes.

nodes.name: Relativized set algebra on $W$ is atomic and representable
nodes.statement: The relativized set algebras based on $M$, but permitting as assignments satisfying formulas only $n$ sequences in $W$ will be an atomic representable algebra.
assumptions: permitting as assignments satisfying formulas only $n$ sequences in $W$
conclusions: will be an atomic representable algebra.

nodes.name: Algebra $\A$
nodes.statement: This algebr, call it $\A$, has universe $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n\}$ where $\phi^M=\{s\in W: M\models \phi[s]\}.$ (This is not representable by its definition because its unit is not a square.) Here $\phi^M$ denotes the permitted asignments satisfyng $\phi$ in $M$.

nodes.name: Completion $\C$ of $\A$ is not representable
nodes.statement: Its completion is the relativized set algebra $\C$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$, which turns out not representable. (All logics are taken in the above signature). The isomorphism from $\Cm\At\A$ to $\C$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$.
nodes.statement_short: The completion of $\A$ is the set algebra $\C$ of $L^n_{\infty,\omega}$-definable sets, which is not representable; $\Cm\At\A\cong\C$.
assumptions: Its completion is the relativized set algebra $\C$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$,
conclusions: which turns out not representable.
The isomorphism from $\Cm\At\A$ to $\C$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$.

nodes.name: Hodkinson's construction as split and blur
nodes.statement: Let us formulate this construction in the context of split and blur. Take the $n$ disjoint copies of $N\times \omega=\G$. Let $a\in \G\times n$. Then $a\in N\times \omega\times n$. Then for every $(a,i)$ where $a\in N\times \omega$, and $i<n$, we have an atom $R_{a,i}^{\M}\in \A$. The term algebra of $\A$ is generated by those. Hence $\N\times \omega\times n$ is the atom structure of $\A$ which can be weakly represented using the $n$ blurs, namely the set $\{\rho, i): i<n\}$. The clique $N$ appeas on the complex algebra level, forcing a finite $N$ colouring, so that the complex algebra cannot be representable.
nodes.statement_short: The atoms $N\times\omega\times n$ are weakly represented with $n$ blurs $(\rho,i)$, while the clique $N$ reappears in the complex algebra.

nodes.name: Infinite $N$ gives complete representability
nodes.statement: We note that if $N$ is infinite, then the complex algebra (which is the completion of the algebra constructed as above ) will be representable and so $\A$, together the term algebra will be completely representable.

nodes.name: Relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$
nodes.statement: We use the graph $N\times \omega$ of countably many disjoint $N$ cliques. We define a relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$ of the form $(\{1'\}\cup (\G\times n), R_{1'}, \breve{R}, R_;)$. The only identity atom is $1'$. All atoms are self converse, so $\breve{R}=\{(a, a): a \text { an atom }\}.$ The colour of an atom $(a,i)\in \G\times n$ is $i$. The identity $1'$ has no colour. A triple $(a,b,c)$ of atoms in $\alpha(\G)$ is consistent if $R;(a,b,c)$ holds. Then the consistent triples are $(a,b,c)$ where \begin{itemize} \item one of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and the other two are equal, or \item none of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and they do not all have the same colour, or \item $a=(a', i), b=(b', i)$ and $c=(c', i)$ for some $i<n$ and $a',b',c'\in \G$, and there exists at least one graph edge of $G$ in $\{a', b', c'\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Atom structure on $\{1'\}\cup(\G\times n)$, all atoms self-converse, with consistent triples defined by colours and graph edges.
differentia: one of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and the other two are equal, or
none of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and they do not all have the same colour, or
$a=(a', i), b=(b', i)$ and $c=(c', i)$ for some $i<n$ and $a',b',c'\in \G$, and there exists at least one graph edge of $G$ in $\{a', b', c'\}$.

nodes.name: Atom structure of $\A$ is isomorphic to the basic matrices ${\cal M}_n$
nodes.statement: $\alpha(\G)$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure. It is exactly the same as that used by Hirsch and Hodkinson, except that we use $n$ colours, instead of just $3$. This allows the relation algebra to have an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis and, in fact, the atom structure of $\A$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha(\G)$ is a relation atom structure with an $n$-dimensional cylindric basis, and the atom structure of $\A$ is isomorphic to ${\cal M}_n$.
assumptions: we use $n$ colours, instead of just $3$.
conclusions: $\alpha(\G)$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure.
This allows the relation algebra to have an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis

the atom structure of $\A$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha(\G)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism with ${\cal M}_n$
nodes.statement: Indeed, for each $m \in {\cal M}_n, \,\ \textrm{let} \,\ \alpha_m = \bigwedge_{i,j<n} \alpha_{ij}. $ Here $ \alpha_{ij}$ is $x_i = x_j$ if $ m_{ij} = 1$' and $R(x_i, x_j)$ otherwise, where $R = m_{ij} \in L$. Then the map $(m \mapsto \alpha^W_m)_{m \in {\cal M}_n}$ is a well - defined isomorphism of $n$-dimensional cylindric algebra atom structures.
nodes.statement_short: Send each basic matrix $m$ to the formula $\alpha_m=\bigwedge_{i,j}\alpha_{ij}$ and check the map is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Complex algebra of $\alpha(\G)$ is not representable
nodes.statement: It can be shown that the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable, because its chromatic number is finite; indeed it is exactly $N$. (This will be demonstrated below.)
conclusions: the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable,
its chromatic number is finite; indeed it is exactly $N$.

nodes.name: Is the constructed relation algebra outside $S\Ra\CA_{n+2}$?
nodes.statement: But we want more. Is it possible, thatthe constructed relation algebrais {\it not} in $S\Ra \CA_{n+2}$ which is strictly smaller that $\RRA$. The idea that could work here, is to use {\it relativized} representations. Algebras in $S\Ra\CA_{n+2}$ do posses representations that are only {\it locally} square. So is the blurring, using $n$ colours, based on $N$, namely $(\rho, i)$ $i<n$, enough to prohibit the complex algebra to be representable in a {\it weaker} sense, which means that we have to strengthen our conditions, involving the superscrit $2$ in the equation with $N$ and $n$. We have $N\geq n(n-1)/2$ but we need a further combinatorial property relating the triple $(2, N, n)$
nodes.statement_short: Can the complex algebra be kept out of $S\Ra\CA_{n+2}$ (no relativized, locally square representation) by a further combinatorial condition on $(2,N,n)$?

nodes.name: Finite-infinite discrepancy for relativized representations
nodes.statement: In any event, there is a finite-infinite discrepancy here, as well, no matter what kind of representation we consider, the base has to be infinite. A representation maps the complex algebra into the powerset of a set of ordered pairs, with base $X$, thae latter has to be infinite. At the same time the graph has an $N$ coloring, and this can be used to partition the complex algebra into $(N\times n)+1$ blocks.

nodes.name: Failure of the classical argument for relativized representations
nodes.statement: But this is not enough; the idea in the classical case, works because one member of the partition induced by the finite colouring will be monochromatic, and will satisfy $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$, which is a contradiction. The last condition is not guaranteed when we have only relativized representations, because if $h$ is such a representation, it is not really a faithful one, in the sense that it can happen that there are $x_0, x_1,x_2\in X$, and $(x_0,x_1)\in h(a)$, $(x_1, x_2)\in h(b)$, $(x_0, x_2)\in h(c)$, and $a, b, c\in \Cm\G$, but $h((a;b).c)=0$ if the node $x_1$ witnessing composition, lies outside the $n$ clique determined by $x_0, x_2$, This cannot happen in case of classical representation. Finite clique is the measure of {\it squareness}. It will be defined shortly.
nodes.statement_short: Classically a monochromatic block gives $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$, a contradiction; relativized representations need not witness composition.

nodes.name: Complex algebra lies outside some $S\Ra\CA_{n+k}$
nodes.statement: But we are also {\it certain } that the complex algebra is not in $S\Ra\CA_{n+k}$ for some $k\in \omega$, by the neat embedding theorem for relation algebras, namey, $\RRA=\bigcap_{k\in \omega}S\Ra\CA_{n+k}.$
conclusions: the complex algebra is not in $S\Ra\CA_{n+k}$ for some $k\in \omega$,

nodes.name: Neat embedding theorem for relation algebras
nodes.statement: $\RRA=\bigcap_{k\in \omega}S\Ra\CA_{n+k}.$
nodes.origin_citation: neat embedding theorem for relation algebras (classical; no reference given in the paper)

nodes.name: Role of the condition $N\geq n(n-1)/2$
nodes.statement: Now, accordingly, let us keep $k$ loose, for the time being. We want to determine the least such $k$. Remember that we required that $N\geq n(n-1)/2$, this was necessary to show that permutations of $\omega\cap \{\rho\}$ induces $n$ back and forth systems of partial isomorphisms of size less than $n$ in our limiting labelled graph $M$, showing that is {\it strongly} $n$ homogeneous, when viewed as a model for the language $L$. This in turn enabled us to show that the term algebra is representable. The plan is to go on with the proof and see what other combinatorial properties one should impose on the relationship between $N$, $n$ and now $k$ to prohibit even {\it a relativized representation}. Obviously one should keep the condition $N\geq n(n-1)/2$ not to tamper with the first part of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: $N\geq n(n-1)/2$ makes $M$ strongly $n$-homogeneous, which gives representability of the term algebra; find further conditions on $N,n,k$.

nodes.name: Informal meaning of $n+k$ squareness
nodes.statement: The property of $n+k$ squareness means, then for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, can always be extended to another clique having at most one more element witnessing composition, so that composition can be preserved in the representation, but only locally. It is easier to build such representations; from the game theoretic point of view because $\forall$ moves are restricted by the size of cliques, which means that the chance that exists provide a node witnessing composition is higher.

nodes.name: Simplified Andr\'eka--N\'emeti construction
nodes.statement: Here we turn to our second split and blur construction. It is a simplified version of the proof of Andr\'eka and N\'emeti, except that for a set of blurs $J$, they defined infinitely many tenary relations on $\omega$ with suffixes from $J$, to synchronize the composition operation. This was necessary to show that the required algebras are generated by a single element; here we use one uniform relation, and we sacrifize with this part of the result, which is worthwhile, due to the reduction of the complexity of the proof. We think that our simplified version captures the essence of the blow up and blur construction of Andr\'eka and N\'emeti.

nodes.name: Two partitions: atoms and blurs
nodes.statement: Let $I$ and $J$ be sets, for the time being assume they are finite. We will define two partitions $(H^P: P\in I)$ and $(E^W: W\in J)$ of a given infinite set $H$, using atoms from a finite relation algebra for the first superscripts, and "blurs" (literally) for the second superscript. The blurs do two things. They are just enough to distort the structure of $\bold M$ in the term algebra, but not in its completions, but at the same time they are colours that are necessary for representing the term algebra. Indeed, we use the first partition to show that the complex algebra of our atom structure is not representable, while we use the second to show that the term algebra is representable.
nodes.statement_short: Partition $H$ by atoms of a finite relation algebra (to kill representability of the completion) and by blurs (to represent the term algebra).

nodes.name: Rectangle $H$
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be a finite set with $|I|\geq 6$. Let $J$ be the set of all $2$ element subsets of $I$, and let $$H=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in I, W\in J, P\in W\}.$$

nodes.name: Splitting technique
nodes.statement: The index $i$ here says that we will replace each atom of this relation algebra by infinitely many atoms, that will define an atom structure of a new infinite relation algebra, {\it the desired algebra}. (This is an instance of a technique called {\it splitting}, which involves splitting an atom into smaller atoms. Invented by Andreka, it is very useful in proving non representability results).

nodes.name: $\bold M$ is blurred in the term algebra but not in its completion
nodes.statement: The structure of $\bold M$ will be {\it blown up} by splitting the atoms, then 'blurred' in the term algebra, but it will {\it not} be blurred in the completion of the term algebra. More precisely, $\bold M$ will be a subalgebra of the completion, but it may (and will not be) a subalgebra of the term algebra.

nodes.name: First partition $H^P$
nodes.statement: We now define two finite partitions of the rectangle, namely $H$. For $P\in I$, let $$H^P=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, W\in J, P\in W\}.$$

nodes.name: Blur partition $E^W$
nodes.statement: The $J$s are the blurs, for $W\in J,$ let $$E^W=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in W\}.$$ The singletons will generate this partition up to a `finite blurring'. That is the term algebra will consist of all those $X$ such that $X$ intersects $E^W$ finitely or cofinitely. For each $W\in J$, we have $W\subseteq I$, and so $E^W$ will be the subrectangle of $H$ on the base $W$.
nodes.statement_short: $E^W$ collects the atoms with blur index $W$; the term algebra consists of sets meeting each $E^W$ finitely or cofinitely.

nodes.name: Evenly distributed triples $e(i,j,k)$
nodes.statement: For $i,j,k\in \omega$ $e(i,j,k)$ abbreviates that $i,j,k$ are {\it evenly distributed}, i.e. $$e(i,j,k)\text { iff } (\exists p,q,r)\{p,q,r\}=\{i,j,k\}, r-q=q-p$$

nodes.name: $3,5,7$ evenly distributed, $3,5,8$ not
nodes.statement: For example $3,5,7$ are evenly distributed, but $3,5,8$ are not.

nodes.name: Atom structure $\cal F$
nodes.statement: All atoms are self-converse. This always makes life easier. We define the consistent triples as follows (Involving identity are as usual $(a, b, Id): a\neq b).$ Let $i,j,k\in \omega$, $P,Q,R\in I$ and $S,Z,W\in J$ such that $P\in S$, $Q\in Z$ and $R\in W$. Then the triple $(a_i^{P,S},a_j^{Q,Z}, a_k^{R,W})$ is consistent iff either \begin{enumroman} \item $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset,$ or \item $e(i,j,k)\&P\leq Q;R.$ \end{enumroman} The second says that if $i,j,k$ are $e$ related then the composition of $P$, $Q$ and $R$ existing on those three rows, is defined like $\bold M$. Let $\cal F$ denote this atom structure, ${\cal F}=H\cup \{Id\}$
nodes.statement_short: Atoms $H\cup\{Id\}$, self-converse; $(a_i^{P,S},a_j^{Q,Z},a_k^{R,W})$ is consistent iff $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset$ or $e(i,j,k)$ and $P\leq Q;R$.

nodes.name: Finite relation algebra $\bold M$
nodes.statement: Now, as promised, we choose a (finite) relation algebra $\bold M$ with atoms $I\cup \{1d\}$ such that for all $P,Q\in I$, $P\neq Q$ we have $$P;P=\{Q\in I: Q\neq P\}\cup \{Id\}\text { and } P;Q=H$$
differentia: for all $P,Q\in I$, $P\neq Q$ we have $$P;P=\{Q\in I: Q\neq P\}\cup \{Id\}\text { and } P;Q=H$$

nodes.name: Existence of $\bold M$; it has only finite representations
nodes.statement: Such an $\bold M$ exists It is also known that $\bold M$, if representable, can be only represented on finite sets.
nodes.origin_citation: known result (no reference given in the paper)
conclusions: Such an $\bold M$ exists
$\bold M$, if representable, can be only represented on finite sets.

nodes.name: $\Cm{\cal F}$ not representable, term algebra ${\cal R}$ representable
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item $\Cm{\cal F}$ is a relation algebra that is not representable. \item ${\cal R}$ the term algebra over $\cal F$ is representable. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: The complex algebra of the blow up and blur atom structure $\cal F$ is not representable, while its term algebra is.
assumptions: Let $\cal F$ denote this atom structure, ${\cal F}=H\cup \{Id\}$
conclusions: $\Cm{\cal F}$ is a relation algebra that is not representable.
${\cal R}$ the term algebra over $\cal F$ is representable.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$. Note that $;$ is defined on $\Cm({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of $\Cm F$. But $\Cm F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while $\M$ only on finite ones, hence we are done. \item The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $$\Uf=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ $\Uf$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$ \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: (1) $\bold M$ embeds in $\Cm{\cal F}$ but has only finite representations; (2) build a complete consistent coloured graph of ultrafilters step by step and map $X\mapsto rep(X)$.

nodes.name: Blow up and blur algebra ${\cal R}$
nodes.statement: The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$.

nodes.name: Ultrafilters $U^a$, $U^W$ and $\Uf$
nodes.statement: For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $$\Uf=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ $\Uf$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$.

nodes.name: Consistent triple of ultrafilters
nodes.statement: Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$

nodes.name: Consistent coloured graph
nodes.statement: We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman}

nodes.name: Complete consistent coloured graph
nodes.statement: We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$.
differentia: for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$.

nodes.name: $n$ complex blur (condition (**))
nodes.statement: Our previous construction of the atom structure satisfied (*) satisfies $(\forall a_1\ldots a_3\ b_1\ldots b_3\in I)(\exists W\in J)(a_1;b_1)\cap\ldots (a_3;b_3)\in U^W.$ We strengthen this condition to (**) $$(\forall a_1\ldots a_nb_1\ldots b_n\in I)(\exists W\in J)W\cap (a_1;b_1)\cap\ldots (a_n;b_n)\neq \emptyset.$$ (This is referred to in \cite{Sayed} as an {\it $n$ complex blur for $\bold M$}, our first construction was a $3$ complex blur).
nodes.origin_citation: Sayed Ahmed [Sayed], Completions, complete representations and omitting types (2013)

nodes.name: All $n\times n$ matrices form a cylindric basis of ${\cal R}_n$
nodes.statement: This condition will entail that the set of {\it all} $n$ by $n$ matrices is a cylindric basis on the new relation algebra ${\cal R}_n$ defined as before, with minor modifications.
conclusions: the set of {\it all} $n$ by $n$ matrices is a cylindric basis on the new relation algebra ${\cal R}_n$

nodes.name: Blow up and blur cylindric algebra of dimension $n$
nodes.statement: Now ${\cal R}_n$ is defined by taking $I$ be a finite set with $|I|\geq 2n+2$, $J$ be the set of all $2$ (See the proof) element subsets of $I$. And then define everything as before. The resulting cylindric algebra is also called the blow up and blur {\it cylindric algebra of dimension $n$}, which actually blows up and blurs the $n$ dimensional finite cylindric algebra consisting of $n$ basic matrices of $\bold M$, whch is representable, so such an algebra exists for every $n.$
nodes.definiendum: blow up and blur {\it cylindric algebra of dimension $n$}

nodes.name: Condition (**) gives amalgamation of matrices
nodes.statement: The new condition (**) guarantess the amalgamation property of matrices (corresponding to commutativity of cylindrifiers) which is the essential property of basis.

nodes.name: Strengthening (**) for full neat reducts
nodes.statement: We know that the term algebra is a subneat reduct of an algebra in $\omega$ extra dimensions. But we need a final tick so that the the term cylindric algebra is a {\it full} neat reduct. This requires a yet another strenghthenig of (**) by replacing $\exists$ by $\forall$.

nodes.name: Diagram $M(\bold e,\phi)$
nodes.statement: Now under this stronger condition, let $\B_n$ be the set of basic matrices of our blown up and blurred ${\cal R}_n$. In the first order language $L$ of $(\omega, <)$, which has quantifier elimination, diagrams are defined for each $K\subseteq n$ and $\phi\in L$, via maps $\bold e:K\times K\to {\cal R}_n$. For an atom let $v(a)$ be its ith co-ordinate, or its $i$ th level in the rectangle. The pair $\bold e$ and $\phi$ defines an element in $\Cm\B_n$, called a diagram, that is a set of matrices, defined by $$M(\bold e, \phi)=\{m\in B_n, i,j\in K, m_{ij}\leq \phi(e_{ij},v(m_{ij})\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: For $\bold e:K\times K\to{\cal R}_n$ and $\phi\in L$, the diagram is the set of basic matrices whose entries obey $\phi$ at their levels.

nodes.name: Normal diagram
nodes.statement: A normal diagram is one whose entries are either atoms or finitely many blurs (by (J)), that is elements of the form $E^W$, in addition to the condition that $\phi$ implies $\phi_e$.

nodes.name: Every diagram is a finite union of normal diagrams
nodes.statement: Any diagram can be approximated by normal ones; and atcually it is a finite union of normal diagrams.
conclusions: Any diagram can be approximated by normal ones;
it is a finite union of normal diagrams.

nodes.name: Term algebra $\Bb_n(\bold M, J, e)$
nodes.statement: The term algebra turns, denoted by $\Bb_n(\bold M, J, e)$, consists of those diagrams,

nodes.name: Neat reducts: $\Nr_t\Bb_n\cong\Bb_t$
nodes.statement: and finally we get that that for $t<n$ $$\Nr_t \Bb_n(\bold M, J, e)\cong \Bb_t(\bold M, J, e).$$
conclusions: $$\Nr_t \Bb_n(\bold M, J, e)\cong \Bb_t(\bold M, J, e).$$

nodes.name: Diagrams as blown up and blurred matrices
nodes.statement: Here actually we are also blowing and bluring the finite dimensional cylindric algebra atom consisting of matrices on $\bold M$, we blow up every $n$ dimensional matrix to infinitely many, where each entry is either an atom of the relation algebra or a blur; these are exactly the diagrams.

nodes.name: Affinity between the two constructions
nodes.statement: This construction actually has a lot of affinity with the first model theoretic construction. First they both prove the same thing; the Andreka et all construction proves that in addition the term algebra is a $k$ neat reduct. Now here we are comparing a relation algebra construction with a cylindric algebra one, but the analogy is worthwhile pointing out.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: $\bold M$ plays the role of the clique $N$
nodes.statement: Replace the clique $N$ in Hodkinson's construction by $\bold M$, in this case the term algebra, $\cal R$ is also obtained by replacing every atom by infinitely many ones, and $\bold M$ appears on the global level as a subalgebra of the complex algebra. To this consruction we can also associate a finite graph with finite chromatic number, namely the complete graph on $\bold M$. The blurs are the colours, that correspond to the colours $(\rho, i)$ in Sayed Ahmed 's construction.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Correspondence of the partitions
nodes.statement: In the first case the splitting of the clique $N$, uses just one index, in the second we use two indices, the atoms of $\bold M$ and the blurs. The first partition replaces the use of Ramseys theorem, the second partition, is a devision of the whole splitting into finitely many rectangles, one for each blur. The homogeneous model $M$ in the second construction correspond to the second partition, in the sense that it is {\it not} the base of the representable term algebra, but $W$ is, which is basically obtained by removing the blurs, that are the same time essential in representing it, $W$ thus corresponds to the term algebra of co-finite finite intersections with the second partition, which in turn is representable.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: One index splits $N$; two indices (atoms of $\bold M$, blurs) split $\bold M$; the first partition replaces Ramsey, the second gives the base $W$.

nodes.name: Summary of blow up and blur
nodes.statement: In short, we start up with a finite structure, blow it up, on the term algebra level, using blurs to represent it, but it will not be blurred enough to disappear on the complex algebra level, forcing the latter to be non-representable (due to incompatibility of "a finitenes condition") with the inevitability of representing the complex algebra on an infinite set.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Map between the ingredients of the two constructions
nodes.statement: More formally, we define a function that maps the ingredients of the first construction to that of the second: $$N\mapsto \bold M$$ $$N\times \omega\times n\mapsto \omega\times P\times J$$ In the former case $J'=\emptyset$, the blurs do not appear on this level, in the second spliting all blurs are used. $$\{(\rho , i): i<n \}\mapsto \{ W: W\in J\}.$$ Here in the first case $n$ blurs are needed to represent the new term algebra. In the later it is the number of two elements subsets of $J$. For $\phi\in L^+$, let $\phi^M=\{s\in {}^nM: M\models \phi[s]\}.$ Here we are {\it not} relativizing semantics. $$\{{\phi}^M: \phi \in L\}\mapsto \Cof(E^W)$$ $$\A\mapsto {\cal R}$$ $$\Cm\At\A\to \Cm\At{\cal R}$$
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: Dictionary $N\mapsto\bold M$, $N\times\omega\times n\mapsto\omega\times P\times J$, $(\rho,i)\mapsto W$, $\A\mapsto{\cal R}$ between the two constructions.

nodes.name: Atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu)$
nodes.statement: Let $l\in \omega$, $l\geq 2$, and let $\mu$ be a non-zero cardinal. Let $I$ be a finite set, $|I|\geq 3l.$ Let $$J=\{(X,n): X\subseteq I, |X|=l,n<\mu\}.$$ Let $H$ be as before, i.e. $$H=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in I, W\in J\}.$$ Define $(a_i^{P,S,p}, a_j^{Q,Z,q}, a_k^{R,W,r})$ is consistent ff $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset$ or $ e(i,j,k) \text { and } |\{P,Q,R\}|\neq 1.$ Pending on $l$ and $\mu$, let us call these atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu).$ Then our first example in is just ${\cal F}(2,1).$ If $\mu\geq \omega$, then $J$ as defined above would be infinite, and $\Uf$ will be a proper subset of the ultrafilters. It is not difficult to show that if $l\geq \omega$ (and we relax the condition that $I$ be finite), then $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable, and if $l<\omega$ then $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is not representable. In the former case we have infnitely many colours, so that the chromatic nmber of the graph is infinite, while in the second case the chromatic number is infinite. Informally, if the blurs get arbitarily large, then in the limit, the resulting algebra will be completely representable, and so its complex algebra will be representable. If we take, a sequence of blurs, each finite, but increasing in size we get a sequence of algebras that are not completely representable, and the sequence of their complex algebras will not be representable. The limit of the former, will be completely representable (with an infinite set of blurs); its completion will be the limit of the second sequence of non representable, will be representable. Either construction can be used to achieve this. This phenomena has many reincarnations in the literature. One is the following: It is is nothing more than Monk's classical non finite axiomatizability result; it gives a sequence of non representable algebras whose ultraproduct is completely representable.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: Generalised atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu)$ with blurs of size $l$; $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is representable iff $l$ is infinite, echoing Monk.

nodes.name: Representability of $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to show that if $l\geq \omega$ (and we relax the condition that $I$ be finite), then $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable, and if $l<\omega$ then $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is not representable. In the former case we have infnitely many colours, so that the chromatic nmber of the graph is infinite, while in the second case the chromatic number is infinite.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable for infinite $l$ and not representable for finite $l$.
assumptions: if $l\geq \omega$ (and we relax the condition that $I$ be finite),
conclusions: $\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable,
$\Cm{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is not representable.

nodes.name: Monk's non-finite axiomatizability theorem
nodes.statement: It is is nothing more than Monk's classical non finite axiomatizability result; it gives a sequence of non representable algebras whose ultraproduct is completely representable.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
conclusions: it gives a sequence of non representable algebras whose ultraproduct is completely representable.

nodes.name: $\RRA$ and the elementary closure of ${\bf CRA}$ are not finitely axiomatizable
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item The classes $\RRA$ is not finitely axiomatizable. \item The elementary closure of the class ${\bf CRA}$ is not finitely axiomatizable. \end{enumarab}

conclusions: The classes $\RRA$ is not finitely axiomatizable.
The elementary closure of the class ${\bf CRA}$ is not finitely axiomatizable.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.3
nodes.statement: For the second we use the second construction. Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$. Then $\Cm{\cal D}$ is completely representable. Thus $\Tm{\cal F}(i,1)$ are $\RRA$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also $\Cm{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result. We prove the cylindric case. Take $\G_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of $\A_i$, as constructed above. Then $\Cm \A_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}\Cm\A_i=\Cm(\prod_{i\in \omega}\A_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: Take ultraproducts of ${\cal F}(i,1)$ (resp. of the cylindric algebras on growing cliques): non-representable algebras with representable ultraproduct.

nodes.name: First construction gives the cylindric analogue
nodes.statement: The first construction also works, by using relation algebra atom structures with $n$ dimensional cylindric bases, this will yield the analogous result for cylindric algebras.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Hirsch--Hodkinson: $\Cm\M(\Gamma)$ representable iff $\chi(\Gamma)$ infinite
nodes.statement: The second re-incarnation is due to Hirsch and Hodkinson, it also works for relation and cylindric algebras, and this is the essence. For each graph $\Gamma$, they associate a cylindric algebra atom structure of dimension $n$, $\M(\Gamma)$ such that $\Cm\M(\Gamma)$ is representable if and only if the chomatic number of $\Gamma$, in symbols $\chi(\Gamma)$, which is the least number of colours needed, $\chi(\Gamma)$ is infinite.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: For each graph $\Gamma$ there is an $n$-dimensional atom structure $\M(\Gamma)$ with $\Cm\M(\Gamma)$ representable iff $\chi(\Gamma)$ is infinite.
conclusions: $\Cm\M(\Gamma)$ is representable if and only if the chomatic number of $\Gamma$, in symbols $\chi(\Gamma)$, which is the least number of colours needed, $\chi(\Gamma)$ is infinite.

nodes.name: Hirsch--Hodkinson: strongly representable algebras are not elementary
nodes.statement: Using a famous theorem of Erdos, they construct a sequence $\Gamma_r$ with infinite chromatic number and finite girth, whose limit is just $2$ colourable, they show that the class of strongly representable algebras is not elementary.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
conclusions: they show that the class of strongly representable algebras is not elementary.

nodes.name: Reverse of Monk-like constructions
nodes.statement: Notice that this is a {\it reverse process} of Monk-like constructions, given above, which gives a sequence of graphs of finite chromatic number whose limit (ultarproduct) has infinite chromatic number.

nodes.name: Bad partition
nodes.statement: Some statement fail in $\A$ iff $At\A$ be partitioned into finitely many $\A$-definable sets with certain `bad' properties. Call this a {\it bad partition}.

nodes.name: Monk's result via bad partitions
nodes.statement: A bad partition of a graph is a finite colouring. So Monks result finds a sequence of badly partitioned atom structures, converging to one that is not. As we did above, this boils down, to finding graphs of finite chromatic numbers $\Gamma_i$, having an ultraproduct $\Gamma$ with infinite chromatic number.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map

nodes.name: Strongly representable atom structure
nodes.statement: An atom structure is {\it strongly representable} iff it has {\it no bad partition using any sets at all}.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
differentia: has {\it no bad partition using any sets at all}.

nodes.name: Reduction to graphs with finitely colourable ultraproduct
nodes.statement: So, here, the idea find atom structures, with no bad partitions, with an ultraproduct that does have a bad partition. From a graph Hirsch nad Hodkinson constructed an atom structure that is strongly representable iff the graph has no finite colouring. So the problem that remains is to find a sequence of graphs with no finite colouring, with an ultraproduct that does have a finite colouring, that is, graphs of infinite chromatic numbers, having an ultraproduct with finite chromatic number.

nodes.name: Erd\H{o}s: graphs of large chromatic number and girth
nodes.statement: Indeed, graphs like this can be found using the probabilistic methods of Erdos, for those methods render finite graphs of arbitrarily large chormatic number and girth.
nodes.section: 4.3 The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
conclusions: those methods render finite graphs of arbitrarily large chormatic number and girth.

nodes.name: Disjoint unions and ultraproducts of Erdos graphs
nodes.statement: By taking disjoint unions, one {\it can get} graphs of infinite chromatic number (no bad partitions) and arbitarly large girth. A non principal ultraproduct of these has no cycles, so has chromatic number 2 (bad partition).

nodes.name: Formula $\alpha_m$ for a basic matrix
nodes.statement: Indeed, for each $m \in {\cal M}_n, \,\ \textrm{let} \,\ \alpha_m = \bigwedge_{i,j<n} \alpha_{ij}. $ Here $ \alpha_{ij}$ is $x_i = x_j$ if $ m_{ij} = 1$' and $R(x_i, x_j)$ otherwise, where $R = m_{ij} \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: Attach to each basic matrix $m$ the conjunction $\alpha_m$ of atomic formulas.

nodes.name: The map is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Then the map $(m \mapsto \alpha^W_m)_{m \in {\cal M}_n}$ is a well - defined isomorphism of $n$-dimensional cylindric algebra atom structures.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $m\mapsto\alpha^W_m$ is an isomorphism of atom structures.

nodes.name: Assume membership; get a flat, square representation
nodes.statement: Assume for contradiction that $\Cm\alpha(\G)\in S\Ra \CA_{n+k}$, and $k\geq 2$. Then $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ has an $n+k-2$-flat representation $X$ \cite{HHbook2} 13.46, which is $n+k-2$ square \cite{HHbook2} 13.10.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\Cm\alpha(\G)\in S\Ra\CA_{n+k}$; it then has an $(n+k-2)$-flat, square representation.

nodes.name: The relativized representation $h$
nodes.statement: In particular, there is a set $X$, $V\subseteq X\times X$ and $g: \Cm\alpha(\G)\to \wp(V)$ such that $h(a)$ ($a\in \Cm\alpha(\G)$) is a binary relation on $X$, and $h$ respects the relation algebra operations. Here $V=\{(x,y)\in X\times X: (x,y)\in h(1)\}$, where $1$ is the greatest element of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$. We write $1(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in h(1).$
nodes.statement_short: Fix the base $X$, unit $V$ and representation $h$.

nodes.name: Recall squareness
nodes.statement: For any $m<\omega$, let $C_m(X)=\{\bar{a}\in {}^mX: Range(a)\text { is an $m$ clique }\}$, then $n+k-2$ squareness means that that if $\bar{a}\in C_{n+k-2}(X)$, $r,s\in \Cm\G$, $i,j,k<n, k\neq i,j$, and $X\models (r;s)(a_i, a_j)$ then there is $b\in C_{n+k-2}(X)$ with $\bar{b}$ agreeing with $\bar{a}$ except possibly at $k$ such that $X\models r(b_i, b_k)$ and $X\models s(b_k, b_j)$. This is the definition. But it is not hard to show that this is equivalent to the simpler condition that for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, all $x,y\in C$ and $a,b\in \Cm\alpha(\G)$, $X\models (a;b)(x,y)$ there exists $z\in X$ such that $C\cup \{z\}$ is a clique and $X\models a(x,z)\land b(z,y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of $(n+k-2)$-squareness and its clique form.

nodes.name: Finite colouring of $\G$
nodes.statement: Now $\G$ has a finite colouring using $N$ colours. Indeed, the map $f:N\times \omega$ defined by $f(l,i)=l$ is a finite colouring using $N$ colours. For $Y\subseteq N\times \omega$ and $l<n$ define $(Y, k)=\{(a,i,l): (a,i)\in Y\}$, regarded as a subset of $\Cm\G$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the $N$-colouring $f(l,i)=l$ of $\G$ and define the blocks $(Y,k)$.

nodes.name: Finite partition $J$
nodes.statement: The nodes of $N\times \omega$ can be partitioned into sets $\{C_j: j<n\}$ such that there are no edges within $C_j$. Let $J=\{1', (C_j,k): j<N, k<n\}$ Then clearly, $\sum J=1$ in $\Cm\alpha(\G)$, so that $J$ is partition of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ into $N\times n+1$ blocks.
nodes.statement_short: Partition $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ into $N\times n+1$ blocks via independent sets $C_j$.

nodes.name: Apply Ramsey's theorem
nodes.statement: As $J$ is finite, we have for any $x,y\in X$ there is a $P\in J$ with $(x,y)\in h(P)$. Since $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ is infinite then $X$ is infinite. Ramsys's theorem aplies in this context, to allow us to infer, that there are distinct $x_i\in X$ $(i<\omega)$, $J\subseteq \omega\times \omega$ infinite and $P\in J$ such that $(x_i, x_j)\in h(P)$ for $(i, j)\in J$, $i\neq j$. Then $P\neq 1'$.
nodes.statement_short: By Ramsey's theorem infinitely many points have all pairs in one block $P\neq 1'$.

nodes.name: Condition needed on $k$
nodes.statement: The condition we need on $k$, is that if $(x_0, x_1)\in h(a)$, $(x_1, x_2)\in h(b)$ and $(x_0, x_2)\in h(c),$ then $a;b.c\neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: State the needed condition: witnessed triangles force $a;b.c\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Open combinatorial question
nodes.statement: So this prompts: {\it Find a combinatorial relation between $n,k, N$ with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$ that forces $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$. What is the least such $k$? This is formulated for any $P$, but maybe the condition would also force Ramseys theorem to give the right block.}
nodes.statement_short: Pose the question of which relation between $n,k,N$ forces $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Monochromatic elements
nodes.statement: A non -zero element $a$ of $\Cm\alpha(\G)$ is monochromatic, if $a\leq 1'$, or $a\leq (\Gamma,s)$ for some $s<n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define monochromatic elements.

nodes.name: $(P;P)\cdot P=0$
nodes.statement: Now $P$ is monochromatic, and the $C_j$ s are independent, it follows also from the definition of $\alpha$ that $(P;P)\cdot P=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The monochromatic block $P$ satisfies $(P;P)\cdot P=0$, the contradiction.

nodes.name: Item (1): $\Cm{\cal F}$ is not representable
nodes.statement: Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$. Note that $;$ is defined on $\Cm({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of $\Cm F$. But $\Cm F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while $\M$ only on finite ones, hence we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Non-representability of $\Cm{\cal F}$ via the first partition.

nodes.name: Use the first partition
nodes.statement: Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-representability will come from the partition $H^P$.

nodes.name: $\bold M$ embeds in $\Cm{\cal F}$
nodes.statement: Note that $;$ is defined on $\Cm({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of $\Cm F$.
nodes.statement_short: Composition of the $H^P$ mirrors $\bold M$, so $\bold M$ embeds in $\Cm F$.

nodes.name: Finite-infinite contradiction
nodes.statement: But $\Cm F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while $\M$ only on finite ones, hence we are done.
nodes.statement_short: $\Cm F$ needs infinite bases while $\bold M$ only has finite ones.

nodes.name: Item (2): the term algebra is representable
nodes.statement: The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $$\Uf=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ $\Uf$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$
nodes.statement_short: Representability of the term algebra ${\cal R}$ via the blur partition.

nodes.name: Use the second partition; recall ${\cal R}$
nodes.statement: The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Work with the blur partition and the algebra ${\cal R}$ of cofinite intersections.

nodes.name: Ultrafilters $U^a$, $U^W$, $\Uf$
nodes.statement: For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $$\Uf=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ $\Uf$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce principal ultrafilters $U^a$ and non-principal $U^W$.

nodes.name: Consistent triples of ultrafilters
nodes.statement: Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$
nodes.statement_short: Define composition and consistency of ultrafilter triples.

nodes.name: Target conditions (i)-(iii)
nodes.statement: So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to achieving consistency conditions (i)-(iii).

nodes.name: Consistent and complete coloured graphs
nodes.statement: Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$.
nodes.statement_short: Define consistent coloured graphs and completeness.

nodes.name: One-point extension
nodes.statement: We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$
nodes.statement_short: Extend a consistent graph by a new point $z$ realising a consistent triple.

nodes.name: Extension stays consistent
nodes.statement: Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph.
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (i)-(iii) give the blur $W$ and keep the graph consistent.

nodes.name: The map $rep$
nodes.statement: We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$
nodes.statement_short: Define $rep(X)$ from a complete coloured graph.

nodes.name: $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism
nodes.statement: We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters.
nodes.statement_short: Aim: $rep$ is an embedding; it is boolean since labels are ultrafilters.

nodes.name: Identity and converse
nodes.statement: $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph.
nodes.statement_short: $rep$ preserves identity and converse.

nodes.name: $rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y)$
nodes.statement: From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$
nodes.statement_short: Consistency of triangles gives one inclusion for composition.

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion: reduce to finding $F,K$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in \Uf$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases:
nodes.statement_short: Completeness reduces the reverse inclusion to finding ultrafilters $F\ni X$, $K\ni Y$.

nodes.name: Case 1: principal label
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Case $l(u,v)=U^a$.

nodes.name: $a\in X;Y$
nodes.statement: $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$
nodes.statement_short: Unpack $X;Y\in U^a$ as $a\in X;Y$.

nodes.name: Pick $b,c$
nodes.statement: Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Choose atoms $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c$.

nodes.name: Case 2: non-principal label
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$
nodes.statement_short: Case $l(u,v)=U^W$.

nodes.name: Infinite intersection with $E^W$
nodes.statement: $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$.
nodes.statement_short: Unpack $X;Y\in U^W$.

nodes.name: Both $X$ and $Y$ finite
nodes.statement: Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i).
nodes.statement_short: Finite $X,Y$: use condition (i).

nodes.name: One of $X,Y$ infinite
nodes.statement: Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$
nodes.statement_short: Infinite $X$: use condition (ii) with a non-principal $U^S$.

nodes.name: $rep$ is one to one
nodes.statement: Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity: every atom is realised, so $rep$ is an embedding.

nodes.name: Ultraproduct ${\cal D}$
nodes.statement: For the second we use the second construction. Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a non-trivial ultraproduct ${\cal D}$ of the ${\cal F}(i,1)$.

nodes.name: Relation algebra case
nodes.statement: Then $\Cm{\cal D}$ is completely representable. Thus $\Tm{\cal F}(i,1)$ are $\RRA$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also $\Cm{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Non-(completely) representable algebras with (completely) representable ultraproduct.

nodes.name: Cylindric case: growing cliques
nodes.statement: We prove the cylindric case. Take $\G_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of $\A_i$, as constructed above.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\G_i$ = disjoint unions of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$.

nodes.name: Ultraproduct is representable
nodes.statement: Then $\Cm \A_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}\Cm\A_i=\Cm(\prod_{i\in \omega}\A_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.
nodes.statement_short: Each $\Cm\A_i$ is non-representable but their ultraproduct is representable.
